title: Master Class | Caro-Kann Exploration | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We take Black and play the Caro-Kann, c6.
White plays the unusual e5 — rare, but not terrible. We can't play ...d5 now, and White could later push d4 into an Advance Caro.
To leave White no advantage at all, we hit the pawn at once with d6, simply trading it off — the simplest response.
White captures on d6.
We recapture — the position is dead equal.
White plays d4. It's a bone-dry, equal position — White isn't fighting for anything, and sometimes you just accept that.
We can play ...d5 now or later; first we develop the knight to f6.
White plays c3. After ...d5 we reach a symmetrical structure where we're effectively playing the white side, a tempo up.
So we push d5, opening a path for the bishop to d6.
White pins with the bishop to g5. There's no single right answer here — but learning to handle dry positions well matters.
The simplest is the bishop to e7, breaking the pin.
White develops the knight to f3. With the pin gone we can play ambitiously — the knight to e4 centralizes and forces White to resolve the tension — or castle first; it hardly matters.
We choose the knight to e4, introducing an asymmetry — ...Bg4 would just be met by the bishop to e2 and stay too symmetrical.
White retreats the bishop to f4 — a surprise; I expected the trade on e7.
We don't change our plan and simply castle.
White develops the bishop to d3. Notice we held our own bishop back to see where his went — a subtle posturing, making the opponent show his cards first.

We play the bishop to g4 — no need to defend the e4-knight, our pawn supports it. This makes White waste a tempo retreating to e2, a small annoyance. The plan is patient: the knight comes to d7, pinning White's f3-knight to the queen, and we build pressure inch by inch.
White castles. You can't do everything at once — you pile on pressure by degrees, and small problems eventually coalesce into big ones.

We complete development with the knight to d7, keeping ...f5 in reserve. When White loses patience with the queen to b3, the point of ...Bg4 pays off — we take on f3. Even a b7-pawn sacrifice would be worth it, but we needn't: the knight to d6 defends b7, and if White grabs both, his king is stripped bare. A mating tip: drive the king in first with a queen check on g5 — before the tempting queen to h4 — then the queen to f4 sets up the battery and mate; the check first stops the defender making luft with the rook.

A note for White: to avoid all this, start with the knight to d2 so ...Ne4 has no bite, then the knight to f3 and bishop to d3 — dead equal. And simply trading on e7 was better than the passive bishop to f4.
